creator: Hank Green
title: Why Aren't Salt-Water Fish Salty?
full_text:
So, every week before we record Dear
Hank and John, I call my research
assistant to Bokey to go over listener
questions. And recently, we hit one from
Odin, who asked whether ocean mammals
drink seawater.
>> The answer to that question is very
basically, no. Whales mostly get water
from their prey, which have fresh water
inside of them. But that raises another
question, which I then asked to Bokey. I
said, "Wait, does that mean that ocean
fish aren't salty?" And to Bokey, who is
smarter than me, said, "Hank, you've
eaten them. You know that they aren't
salty. They are definitely not as salty
as the ocean. I have to salt my salmon."
So, I said, "Good point, to Bokey. Uh
but also, why? Why? They live in the
ocean. Seems like the simple thing to do
would just be ocean on the inside,
because I know how energetically
expensive it is to pump ions around. A
huge, huge percentage of the energy that
you consume, like the food that you ate,
a huge amount of it goes toward just
maintaining ion gradients across cells.
Not even doing anything with those
gradients, just maintaining them at
rest.
>> That's a huge percentage of your at-rest
metabolism.
>> And a saltwater fish can only be not
salty if it spends its entire life
preventing that from happening. Fish
need to spend a tremendous amount of
energy to keep the ocean outside of
themselves, like keep themselves from
becoming ocean. And maybe this doesn't
sound so weird to you, but they've been
in the ocean for a long time. The easy
thing would just be to have your inside
have the same concentration of particles
as the outside. And this is actually
sharks do this. Sharks do it not by
having salt on the inside of them, but
by building up a lot of urea in their
tissues. And that makes the water
osmotic gradient less intense. But bony
fish don't do this. Now, if you watched
my video on the hardest problem
evolution ever solved, you know that
bony fish first evolved in fresh water.
So, that was my first thought. Does that
mean that bony fish aren't salty because
they evolved first in fresh water, and
they just never fixed that? No. Now, it
might be that they don't do the urea
thing that sharks do because they
evolved in fresh water. But sharks also
don't do the thing where they have the
same amount of like sodium chloride on
the inside as the outside. Nobody's
doing that. So, there must be a reason
why. I got to explain osmosis in a
little more detail now, and I apologize
for having introduced that in a sort of
slapdash way. I know most people don't
get osmosis. I barely do. If water can
cross a membrane more easily than the
dissolved stuff in the water, then water
tends to move toward the side with the
more dissolved material. So, basically,
if there's two groups of something and
they can pass through a membrane,
physics wants there to be the same
amount of everything on both sides of
that membrane. Now, if the water can
pass through the membrane more easily
than the particles in the water on one
side or the other, then the water will
move across the membrane to the side
with more dissolved material. And since
there's way more material in the ocean
than in a fish, that means that water's
going to get sucked out of fish.
Seawater is about 35 g of salt per
liter. A typical marine bony fish keeps
its internal fluids around a third of
that. ocean has more dissolved stuff
than fish, and that means water's going
to tend to leave the fish and move into
the ocean, which is a ridiculous problem
to have. And yet they do have it. If
there's one thing I know about problems
that are really big and haven't been
solved, it's that they can't be solved.
Or like, they can't be solved by the
existing systems. So, there's a reason
why this problem exists because you
could fix the osmosis problem by just
having more salt inside of the body. But
they don't do that. Instead, there's a
huge amount of work that goes into
keeping the inside of the fish
relatively fresh water. And this is hard
because gills have to be thin and wet
and full of blood because they exchange
oxygen and carbon dioxide with the
surrounding water. Any structure that is
good at exchanging oxygen and carbon
dioxide is also going to be really good
at exchanging other stuff, including
having water flow out of it. You can't
really have one of those things without
the other. So, like, the gills are a bit
of a problem, which is that basically
gills are just shooting out fresh water
all the time. And fish need to have
them. Now, they have some mechanisms for
slowing that down, but they can't slow
it down completely. So, what do they do?
What do the fish do? They drink. They
drink sea water, which of course I can't
do because it would kill me. The amount
of water that it takes for my body to
filter the salt out would be greater
than the amount of water that I get from
the sea water, which would mean it
dehydrates me until the point where I
would die unless I got fresh water. But
this is a solvable problem. You could do
a few things. You can filter it out more
effectively with the kidneys. And also,
you can have things in the gills called
mitochondrion-rich cells or ionocytes,
which are cells that have a lot of
mitochondria in them. Why? So that they
can produce a lot of ATP. Mitochondria,
what are they? The powerhouse of the
cell. They produce a ton of this ATP,
and that ATP goes to work pumping
chloride across the gill membrane out of
the body. So then, the gill becomes
useful. Basically, the water inside of
the fish is going to be more saline than
it would like, and it's going to be
pumping that salt out constantly to try
and keep the water inside of the fish
more fresh. So all that's happening, a
huge amount of energy is being spent,
and we are back to the original
question. Why? Why keep paying for all
of this? Why not evolve to just have
more salt inside and reduce the osmotic
pressure? Why not just have ocean in
you? The answer is what I was saying
before. Animals like us, vertebrates, we
spend a huge amount of our energy
maintaining ion gradients. So right now,
there's a certain kind of concentration
inside of the cell and a certain
concentration outside of the cell.
Sodium is generally kept high on the
outside of cells and low on the inside
of cells. And so if the outside of cells
sodium goes up, just have there still be
the same difference between the outside
of the inside, but raise the whole thing
up. That would allow for all of the
stuff that gets done by having this
gradient across the membrane, which we
use for all kinds of stuff, for
signaling and for making your muscles
work. I am intentionally avoiding some
details here. Just know that the the
difference is important. And then
potassium is in general kept higher on
the inside of cells and lower on the
outside and that allows it to like open
up channels and have it flow out and
that does stuff. You could have all
those gradients move up, the
differential would still be the same.
And evolution can change the internal
salinity of an animal. Marine fish are
more saline in their tissues than I am,
but evolution cannot simply raise a
fish's salinity to match seawater
without changing a bunch of other
systems at the same time and also
possibly breaking proteins. Seawater
strength salt concentrations would
affect the membranes, the pumps, the
enzymes, the nerves, the muscles, the
kidneys, the gills, development, cell
volume. Basically, matching the outside
would reduce this one big problem, but
it would create so many other problems
that fish have never solved this problem
and it it's possible that it's not
solvable. Like the concentration of salt
that this would require inside of
tissues would make it so that proteins
couldn't fold into all of the shapes
that they need to fold into for a fish
to exist. So there's one way of
imagining this, which is kind of like a
good example would be the voltage of a
house. Like you can't just change the
voltage of a house without also having
to replace all the appliances. But you
could change the voltage of a house if
you figured out like how to slowly
change the voltage and slowly change the
appliances at the same time, which seems
like something evolution could solve.
And so that first thing might be the
case. Fish biologists, please let me
know which one you think it is. It's not
entirely clear to me, but I think that
it might be more the second one, which
is that you can't change the voltage of
the house to a voltage so high that if
you plug anything into it, it will just
break. Now there are organisms that live
at much higher salt concentrations
inside of their bodies. Microbes are
adapted to extremely salty environments,
but they're microbes and also their
proteins and membranes and enzymes, they
have all adapted to those conditions.
Now, the question is, could that happen
to a fish? And I think the answer
probably is no. This is also true of
like depth. I should make a video about
this, but fish can only go so deep. Like
the ocean is deeper than fish can go,
which is awesome. There's a depth beyond
which a fish can live, and the reason
why is that the pressure makes it so
that proteins don't fold normally. And
that's not just a oh I we need to evolve
to have our proteins fold differently
kind of problem. It seems like it seems
like it's a proteins can't fold into all
of the ways that they would need to fold
into for there to be complex
multicellularity
in these conditions. I think that also
might be the case for the literal
saltiness of seawater.
Now, I'm not sure about this,
but it's one of those two things. It's
either the appliances can't evolve along
with the voltage fast enough, or the
voltage is so high that anything that
would do the job of a light bulb or a
washing machine would break. Now, there
is also the shark way around this
problem, where you get closer to the
ocean's osmotic pressure, but you do
that by filling yourself with something
that isn't salt, that isn't as active in
the biology of an organism. They retain
a lot of urea, which increases the
concentration of dissolved material in
their bodies, and helps them hold onto
water. But, urea can destabilize
proteins, so sharks also have TMAO,
which helps protect proteins from urea.
And salt also still leaks in, so sharks
have to have a rectal gland that removes
excess salt. And that's a totally
separate way of removing salt than the
way that bony fish do it, which is again
why
sharks are not fish. You've heard me
here before, folks. It's just crazy to
me that like just be salty is so hard
that instead like most probably not
most, but a huge percentage of the
calories burned in the ocean are burned
keeping the fish freshwater on the
inside, which is the only way that
whales can exist. You probably have
heard the term homeostasis, this idea
that living things have to maintain a
bunch of like overlapping ways of being
and that they're maintaining inside of
themselves that make themselves
possible. Temperature, acidity, glucose,
oxygen, carbon dioxide, the amount of
water, all of the ion gradients are a
part that you don't get in high school.
You might get a little bit of it, but
man, it's it's most of it. It's wild. We
are maintaining these ion gradients and
they are the only way that the cells can
communicate with each other to make the
system work. They're not the only way.
They're one of the main ways that the
cells communicate with each other to
make the system work. I mean, so much of
the nervous system works that way. You
know, you mess with that, everything
falls apart. But life is not just
building a body once. Almost everything
is maintenance here. It's maintaining
the conditions in which the body can
keep working. Saltwater fish are not
salty because their muscle was never a
bag of seawater. The fish prevent that
from happening because otherwise the
muscles don't muscle. They don't do the
work. They fall apart. Like the proteins
might denature. And then, crazy
activity. When I get a piece of cod,
I put a bunch of salt on it. Cuz if I
just drank distilled water all day and
never got any salt, I would die. We need
extra salt as land animals. And fish
that live in salt in fresh water also
need extra salt. They have the opposite
problem. There's a range of salinity at
which it works and outside of that range
apparently it's just really hard to make
it work. So the fish is working its
whole life to not become ocean. It's
trying to stay fish, which is honestly
also what I'm trying to do. Now, there's
something really interesting going on
here that I realized because I was
working on this script the same time I
was working on this script about no
effort being wasted. Is there a tension
here? Because of course evolution is
going to optimize for the least amount
of effort possible. So, adding effort
seems like, why would we do that?
Likewise, there were a lot of comments
on the video that were like, "Hey, it's
hilarious that you're making a video
about how no effort is wasted and then
you talk about how you do pre-orders
specifically so that you don't waste a
bunch of effort in the form of like
money and time and cotton like making
shirts that people don't buy. So, is
there a difference between those two
things? I've thought about this a bunch.
The difference here is that the systems
you're seeing here, the fish in the
water, the t-shirt pre-sales, they are
the way in which previous effort wasn't
wasted. They are the result of previous
moments of friction and that friction
was not wasted because it resulted in
better optimized systems. In the case of
the pumps on the gills of the fish, this
was optimized through evolution. So,
they couldn't get into the saline water
from the fresh water without optimizing
these systems, without creating a way to
do this, without making it easier to
live in salt water. And so, through
natural selection, they got these new
traits. In the case of the t-shirt
pre-order, a new trait evolved through
human learning. We did it one way, we
didn't like how that was going, we
thought how else could we do it and we
did it the new way where the shirts are
only available for 2 weeks, there's only
3 days left and we developed that
system. That it means that if you order
the shirt in the next 3 days, we will
then at the end of those 3 days order
the shirts and then when they get
printed, we'll send them out to you.
During a weird moment of that video, I
said something that probably just
sounded like a silly thing to say,
"Tonight we feast on the labor of
centuries. Tonight we feast on the labor
of centuries. Mole cult, no effort is
wasted." [music] And in that context, it
was just a silly thing to say. But, this
is actually a very important sentence
for me. It's something that my friend
Joda George said to me years and years
ago before we went on stage to play a
show.
What a great thing to say right before
you go on stage to play a show, right?
It hit me very hard. I thought about it
all night. It's more than 10 years
later, I'm still thinking about it.
Maybe I should make a whole tonight we
feast on the labor of centuries video.
But really, it's not centuries, it's
eons. The effort of the fish to survive
and also evolution selecting for fish
that were more successful, are all in
service of something. And often, that
thing is
optimization. It's making a hard thing
easier, but that's not so that we can do
less. It is so that we can do more. And
that's where we are right now, like
doing more. We are feasting on the labor
of centuries. And I don't want to leave
off that like people 100 years ago were
feasting on the labor of centuries, and
the people 100 years before that. We've
been building the whole time. I don't
know, it's complex. There's both a
tension between no effort is wasted and
tonight we feast on the labor of
centuries, and a way in which they
complement each other. So like I, for
example, do not crave threshing wheat. A
world in which I spent a large portion
of my life threshing wheat would be a
way more effortful life, but it would
not be a better life. At the same time,
the effort of those people who did the
threshing of the wheat was very
important to me existing now. Like
figuring out how they were going to do
that work. Like we are still benefiting
from that labor. And so what that means
to me is that we still have to find our
stretch now. We still have to find the
ways in which like inside of our nature,
we can exert effort into the world in a
way that builds something, so that the
labor that future humans feast on will
be the labor that we are doing right
now. They will feast upon our labor, and
they will in turn turn that into yet
more beautiful and more peculiar things.
No effort is wasted. Tonight we feast on
the labor of centuries. Mole Cult.
Too weird to fail.

notes.note: Sharks are fish — specifically cartilaginous fish (Class Chondrichthyes). Bony fish (Osteichthyes) are the other major fish group. The osmoregulation difference described distinguishes sharks from bony fish, but doesn't remove them from the fish category.
notes.claim: Hank Green considers sharks to not be fish (i.e., they are not bony fish).

sources.quote: Modern sharks are classified within the division Selachii[1] and are the sister group to the Batomorphi (rays and skates).
sources.explanation: Provides the scientific classification mentioned in the note.

sources.quote: chondrichthian, (class Chondrichthyes), any member of the diverse group of cartilaginous fishes that includes the sharks
sources.explanation: Confirms sharks are part of the cartilaginous fish class.

sources.quote: The class is one of the two great groups of living fishes, the other being the osteichthians, or bony fishes.
sources.explanation: Supports the note's claim about the two major fish groups (cartilaginous and bony).
